source_metadata.title: The Dragon Hatchling: The Missing Link between the Transformer and Models of the Brain
source_metadata.source_type: arXiv preprint / AI-ML architecture and theory paper

atoms.canonical_statement: The study introduces BDH and BDH-GPU to connect Transformer-like attention-based language modeling with local graph dynamics that admit a neuron/synapse interpretation.
The theoretical program uses computational complexity and distributed-computing reductions to relate macro-level attention mechanisms to local particle and graph dynamics.
The paper provides a public code repository link and includes a self-contained BDH-GPU PyTorch listing in Appendix E, except that RoPE implementation is left to the user.
The authors do not provide a direct account of how the brain transfers fast inference state into longer-term memory beyond the shorter time scales modeled here.

source_anchor.paragraph: Implications for learning dynamics of natural lifelong inference systems

atoms.canonical_statement: The paper states that grounding the proposed reasoning kernels more deeply in brain-science findings and validating them experimentally are future steps rather than objectives completed in this work.

BDH is defined as an n-neuron local graph system whose trainable parameters are graph topology/edge weights and whose fast inference state is represented by edge reweighting on synapse-like connections.
BDH inference executes a four-round local kernel per layer; for L layers, new tokens are introduced every 4L rounds and readout occurs after another 4L-round cycle.
The local BDH interaction protocol in Table 1 is formally equivalent to the vector/tensor state-space dynamics given by Equation 6.
The BDH local ruleset can be expressed using positive neuron state, Hebbian learning, excitatory and inhibitory circuits, and thresholding.

The authors argue that Hebbian learning combined with neural circuits is plausibly sufficient for language and reasoning at brain scale over minute-scale inference, but this is a mechanistic hypothesis rather than direct neuroscience validation.

BDH-GPU is obtained by low-rank factorization of graph transitions followed by ReLU, linear-attention access to low-rank state rather than materializing the full synapse matrix, and LayerNorm normalization.
BDH-GPU(n,d) stores nearly all trainable weights in E, Dx, and Dy and therefore has (3+o(1))nd parameters; the main scaling dimension is neuron count n while d is kept much smaller.
Vanilla BDH-GPU uses shared weights across L recurrent layers, an n-by-d recurrent attention state for each layer, and no fixed context-window boundary in its state-space formulation.

For any low-rank feed-forward matrix product DE, the paper constructs BDH neuron-interaction graphs with O(nd) parameters that realize the same transformation; arbitrary such graph transformations need not admit an exact low-rank converse.
The paper claims that BDH can express the BDH-Normfree attention block with a sparse synapse graph containing O(nd) edges after suitable preparation of attention values.
Combining Claims 3 and 4, the authors conclude that BDH is at least as expressive as BDH-GPU at the same asymptotic parameter count O(nd) and state size O(nd) per layer.

The scaling study trained decoder-only models on a mixed Europarl language-modeling/translation stream using raw UTF-8 bytes, truncated backpropagation through time, temporally coherent minibatches, and recurrent state carried between minibatches.

For the main scaling comparison, all model sizes used En-PL and En-Cs Europarl data totaling 380 MB, saw 1.2 billion tokens (about three epochs), used 2048-token training sequences, AdamW, learning rate 1e-3 with 1000 warm-up steps decaying linearly to 1e-4, adaptive gradient clipping, and weight decay 0.1.

The GPTXL baseline was a GPT2-like Transformer with TransformerXL-style carried KV cache of 4096 entries and ALiBi; depth, embedding size, heads, MLP size, and dropout were tuned/scaled from 25M to 800M parameters.

exposures.details: GPT2-like Transformer with TransformerXL carried KV cache and ALiBi

atoms.canonical_statement: BDH-GPU scaling models used d=256, 8 layers, 4 heads, dropout 0.1, and increased n from 32,768 at 25M parameters to 1,048,576 at 800M parameters.

exposures.details: d=256; 8 layers; 4 heads; dropout=0.1; n scales with model size

atoms.canonical_statement: Figure 7 compares BDH-GPU, gated BDH-GPU prime, and GPTXL under the same training and evaluation regime; BDH models carried recurrent rho state across minibatches while GPTXL carried the latest 4096 KV-cache entries.
Validation loss decreased with model size for all three architectures in Figure 7, and the authors report that gated BDH-GPU prime matched the GPT Transformer across every evaluated model size.

Across the tested next-token-prediction tasks, the authors report that BDH-GPU generally reduced loss faster per training token than the Transformer and identify scarce-data or makespan-sensitive training as favorable settings for the architecture.

The paper gives an inference arithmetic complexity bound of O(ndL) for a simple BDH-GPU implementation and states that for d=256 a state-space linear-attention kernel becomes faster and more memory-efficient than causal attention for contexts typically above 4096 tokens.

The modularity experiment analyzed a 24M-parameter BDH-GPU model with n=32,768, d=256, 4 heads, and 8 layers, thresholding DxE-derived neuron graphs; the experiment was repeated across five independently pretrained random seeds.
For each of the five pretrained models, 3 of 4 encoder heads and all decoder heads followed the expected right-tail parameter distribution, corresponding to 12 of 16 analyzed parameter submatrices.

For the representative 8,192-neuron subgraph thresholded at beta=1.2, 46,820 edges remained; degree distributions were heavy-tailed and power-law-like, and the visualization showed a core-periphery structure.
Thresholded BDH-GPU neuron-interaction matrices exhibited positive Newman modularity that persisted where random-graph and random-low-rank baselines fell toward zero.

The authors conclude that positive-modularity graph structure emerges during training in DxE and DyE and plausibly reflects cluster-aware information propagation induced by the ReLU-lowrank mechanism.

One encoder submatrix in each studied four-head model lacked a heavy positive tail; the authors did not provide a convincing method to isolate negative signal from bias and therefore omitted that case from detailed analysis.

Claim 7 states that n-dimensional linear attention can approximate attention over up to O-tilde(n) key-value pairs under weak-correlation and uniformity assumptions, while a weaker Omega-tilde(sqrt(n)) guarantee is claimed without those assumptions except for negligible inputs.

BDH-GPU has no architectural hard bound on context length, but the authors report that historical-signal damping is needed at long context to control stale-state noise; RoPE plus ALiBi was sufficient in their vanilla experiments.

The monosemantic-synapse experiment used an 8-layer BDH-GPU model with n=49,152, d=256 and 4 heads, trained on about one epoch of En-Es, En-Pt and En-Fr Europarl data totaling 1.9 billion tokens with 2048-character truncated-BPTT sequences.
The same identified synapses increased activity for country or currency concepts across both French and English contexts, including semantically equivalent expressions using different words.
Currency-related sentences produced substantially higher values on the identified currency synapse than non-currency European-politics sentences, with rank-biserial correlation 0.86 and p<1e-14.

atoms.canonical_statement: The predictability/sparsity experiment trained a BDH-GPU model with n=65,536, d=256 and 4 layers on a synthetic next-token task consisting of a fixed 13-letter warm-up followed by eight repetitions of an 8-letter random word in a 77-letter pattern.

In layer 2 of the synthetic predictability experiment, non-zero activation occupied 4.0%-7.5% of neurons during memorization and approximately 2.5% during repetition; the slow-acting half of RoPE frequency groups showed the largest memorization-to-repetition contrast.

The authors interpret the reduced higher-layer activity for predictable repeated inputs as evidence that BDH neuron activity tracks surprisal and provides a native form of conditional or adaptive computation.

The model-merging experiment trained a 19M-parameter En-Es base model, continued separate copies on En-Fr and En-Pt, then concatenated tensors along neuron dimension n and averaged non-n tensors to create a 38M-parameter merged model with n=49,152; reported merged results used no post-merge finetuning.
Base En-Es achieved validation next-token prediction loss 0.36 on the Es→En Europarl translation direction.

atoms.canonical_statement: Without post-merge finetuning, the concatenated model retained translation from Spanish, French, and Portuguese into English but mixed the three Romance languages when translating from English.
The authors interpret the merging experiment as evidence that BDH-GPU neuron-space representations can support direct model composability by concatenating separately trained parameter blocks.
The no-backpropagation-through-time ablation detached K and V in the LinearAttention implementation to block temporal gradient flow through recurrent attention state.

Models trained without backpropagation through time retained some language-modeling ability but lost cross-language concept matching; English losses were approximately 0.75-1.05 versus about 0.65 for an unconditional English model trained with BPTT.

The authors identify one-dimensional model scaling, locality of parameters/state, direct state explainability, and parameter-space model surgery/composition as the main engineering opportunities of BDH-GPU.

The authors hypothesize that modular scale-free network structure, synaptic plasticity, and Hebbian learning may arise from the core reasoning function itself rather than from specific long-term training dynamics.
The authors propose Axiomatic AI as a direction for reducing risks from unpredictable long-horizon autonomous reasoning by seeking principled micro-foundational accounts of model dynamics.
